lesson.title: Project clinic: trustworthy baselines and measurements
lesson.short: Workload design · tuning fairness · latency · uncertainty
lesson.timeMeaning: Suggested independent study minutes; not scheduled contact time
lesson.lead: A result is only as convincing as the comparison that produced it. Design the evaluation before you optimize the system.
goals: Choose baselines that isolate the claimed improvement.
Distinguish workload-total, per-query and tail metrics.
Design repeatable timing, split and timeout policies.

sections.title: Start here: prerequisites and course status
sections.html:
Some queries improve and one gets slower. Has the system improved? We will calculate the total before choosing a summary, then design a measurement that cannot hide the slow query.

Bring the bounded question from lesson 32. All timings below are original hypothetical examples. This clinic is supplemental practice, not an Edinburgh lecture or verified Canvas assignment; instructor deliverables, assessment rules, deadlines and submission arrangements remain unverified.

sections.title: Choose what the baseline is supposed to answer
sections.html:
A baseline must answer a question. A native or widely used system tests practical benefit. A simple heuristic asks whether complexity is necessary. Removing the new component while leaving a coherent system tests its contribution: an ablation. A fastest-measured candidate oracle shows headroom, but its hindsight is not deployable performance.

For batching, comparing against an untuned server with a different recall target leaves several explanations for a win. Match resources, quality, dataset, splits and tuning effort; label defaults as defaults. Pin versions and verify correct results first. If code is reimplemented, disclose that and test its relevant behavior.

Write workload conditions next to the baseline: sizes, selectivity, skew, join pattern, concurrency, reads/writes, freshness and cache state. Include the stress condition the claim concerns. A comparison only in a favorable regime cannot establish a broader benefit.

Key takeaway

A strong baseline removes alternative explanations for a win.

sections.title: Worked example: aggregate speedup can reverse the story
sections.html:
Take two baseline times, 1 s and 100 s. Proposed times are 0.5 s and 110 s. Query speedups are 1/0.5=2 and 100/110≈0.909. Their arithmetic mean is (2+0.909)/2≈1.455; the geometric mean is √(2×0.909)≈1.348. Both exceed one.

Now execute the fixed workload once: baseline=1+100=101 s; proposed=0.5+110=110.5 s. Workload speedup=101/110.5≈0.914, so the workload slows down. Saving 0.5 s cannot pay for losing 10 s. The geometric mean weights query ratios equally on a logarithmic scale; workload total weights actual time. Report which question each answers.

Nine queries save 1 ms each; one loses 100 ms. What is the total change?

Saved=9×1=9 ms; added=100 ms; net=91 ms slower. A “nine of ten wins” count hides magnitude. Show regressions as well as summary ratios.

Tail percentiles also need a declared quantile convention and enough observations. Ten values do not give stable p99 evidence; correlated queries within one run are not independent repetitions.

sections.title: Control the measurement boundary
sections.html:
Draw the request timeline: creation → preprocessing → queue → planning → transfer/execution → final response. Mark the interval timed by each metric. A GPU launch can return before device work finishes, so use suitable synchronization or device events for execution and separately measure complete wall time.

Warm-up can load a model, compile code, populate caches and connect services. If the claim includes startup or elastic scaling, report cold and warm paths. Alternate or randomize system order to reduce drift; log shared-machine activity.

Fix request count/duration, repetitions, warm-up, stopping and failure policy before comparing. A 30-second timeout tells us the run did not finish by 30 seconds; it is censored evidence, not a row to delete or an exact 30-second completion. Report failures and useful lower bounds without inventing finish times.

Sources for this section: NVIDIA cuVS: Benchmarking methodologies. Numerical traces marked original are teaching examples, not reported measurements.

sections.title: Build a minimal evaluation matrix
sections.html:
Begin with a tiny smoke test checking installation and correct outputs. Then expand a small matrix only along axes that challenge the claim: perhaps two sizes, easy/typical/stress workloads, two resource limits and a validation-only parameter sweep. The full cross-product can be expensive without answering a better question.

Choose split units from intended generalization: template for learned optimization, source document/entity for extraction, time for future workloads. ANN needs exact reference neighbors under the same metric and eligible set. A cloud prototype needs commit/recovery validation separately from timing.

Keep raw runs and exclusion reasons. Environment outages and method crashes are different, but neither should vanish silently.

The baseline gets ten tuning trials and the proposal gets 500. How can this be made fair?

Equalize or justify budgets on separate validation data and report search cost. If that is impossible, disclose the asymmetry and restrict the conclusion. More search alone may explain the chosen operating point.

sections.title: Report uncertainty and make the consultation useful
sections.html:
For a fixed-workload claim, one complete workload run is one experimental repetition. Compare three hypothetical matched pairs: baseline 100,104,98 ms; proposed 98,100,99 ms. Subtract within pairs: savings 2,4,−1 ms. Sum=5 ms; mean saving=5/3≈1.67 ms; range=−1 to 4 ms. One pair regresses. These three pairs are descriptive evidence, not a confidence interval or a broad guarantee.

With justified additional independent pairs, estimate uncertainty for the paired effect. Resample whole pairs if resampling is appropriate; treating every correlated query as independent invents precision. Statistical significance and useful practical size are different questions.

A system is 2% faster and runs vary about 5%. Is there no benefit?

Those percentages alone cannot decide. Inspect independent sample count, paired differences and a suitable interval for the effect. Improve controls or collect justified repetitions if uncertainty remains wide, then judge whether the possible benefit matters in practice.

Bring the baseline table, timeline, one raw trace and evaluation matrix to consultation. Ask which omitted workload most threatens the claim, record actual advice, and apply protocol changes consistently.

Key takeaway

Quality, runtime, resources and failures belong in the same evidence package.

quiz.question: Which report best handles a timed-out query?
options: Remove it from all summaries.
Count it as zero seconds.
Report the timeout threshold and failure count, and avoid pretending the exact runtime is known.
Replace it with the median successful runtime.
quiz.explanation: A timeout gives censored information. Dropping it can systematically hide regressions.

questions.question: Baseline query times are 1 s and 100 s; new times are 0.5 s and 110 s. What happened to the fixed workload total?
options: It improved because one query is 2× faster.
It cannot be computed.
It stayed exactly equal.
It increased from 101 s to 110.5 s.
questions.explanation: Baseline total=1+100=101 s; new total=0.5+110=110.5 s, so the fixed workload is 9.5 s slower. Its speedup is 101/110.5≈0.914. A mean of per-query speedup ratios weights the queries differently and can exceed one while total time grows.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Why distinguish kernel-only timing from end-to-end latency?
options: End-to-end measurement is never meaningful.
Kernel timing always includes all network requests.
To remove every inconvenient cost.
Transfers, queueing, preprocessing and orchestration may dominate user-visible time.
questions.explanation: A local optimization may disappear at the application boundary. Label both measurement scopes.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: Which split best tests generalization to new documents when many chunks come from the same document?
options: Put test labels into every prompt.
Split at the source-document level.
Randomly split chunks from every document across train and test.
Evaluate only the training data.
questions.explanation: Document-level splitting reduces leakage through near-duplicate or related chunks. The split should match the intended unit of generalization.
questions.origin: Original supplemental exercise; not a verified assessed question

questions.question: A 2% speed improvement appears within about 5% run-to-run variation. What is justified?
options: A cautious report with uncertainty and better-controlled or justified repeated measurement.
A guaranteed 2% win on every workload.
Deletion of every slow run.
A claim that all systems are equal.
questions.explanation: The two percentages alone neither establish nor rule out an effect. Inspect independent sample count, paired differences where appropriate, and uncertainty; then judge practical importance.
